text:
alex_ng: Heads-up — I ran a quick apples-to-apples between streaming and non-streaming on the v2 runtime. Seeing weird regression with chunking/backpressure. TL;DR: streaming p95 token latency ~220ms, non-streaming p95 ~140ms, throughput similar but CPU/GPU profiles differ. Thoughts?

mira_patel: Thanks. Can you paste the harness config and the exact commands? We need identical model weights, same kv-cache warmup, and same batching heuristics. For streaming tests use --streaming and for non-streaming --blocking. Also ensure client read loop uses 64KB read windows.

alex_ng: Here's the harness and run commands:

```json
{
  "model": "redwood-7b-v1",
  "quant": "q4_0",
  "batch_max_tokens": 2048,
  "batch_policy": "dynamic_latency",
  "kv_warmup": 1000,
  "seed": 42
}
```

Run commands:
```
./harness/replay --replay-file=replays/q3_chat_trace.json --concurrency=32 --mode=streaming --client-read-window=65536
./harness/replay --replay-file=replays/q3_chat_trace.json --concurrency=32 --mode=blocking --batch-window-ms=5
```

perf-bot: PROFILING RESULTS (streaming vs blocking)
streaming: GPU util 72%, CPU load 58%, p50 90ms, p95 220ms, tokens/sec 980
blocking: GPU util 82%, CPU load 45%, p50 70ms, p95 140ms, tokens/sec 1005
notes: streaming shows stalls during chunk flush; KV cache hit-rate 98% both.

jonathan_lee: My suspicion: kernel selection changes based on requested output chunk sizes—streaming forces smaller decode loops so the JIT picks a different GEMM tiling/kernels. Check runtime logs for selected kernel suffixes (fast_gemm32 vs generic_gemm). Also verify kv cache access pattern — streaming interleaves reads with network backpressure.

alex_ng: Found lines:
[runtime] selected kernel=fast_gemm32_tile4 opt_level=2
[runtime] selected kernel=generic_gemm opt_level=1
Switch happens after 512 tokens produced (when chunking switches to 32-token flush).

mira_patel: Can we run forcing flags:
--kernel=fast_gemm32 --force-quant-path
and then compare streaming vs blocking? Also increase batch_max_tokens to avoid dynamic kernel flip.

sam_cooper: On the client side, what's the read-loop pattern? If clients read slowly, streaming stalls and runtime doesn't refill GPU. For apples-to-apples we should use a tight reader that drains bytes immediately.

rachel_wong: I'll tweak replay harness to simulate 'fast-drain' vs 'slow-drain' clients. We should run matrix: {streaming,blocking} x {fast,slow} x {kernel=auto,forced_fast}. That'll surface backpressure impact.

alex_ng: Great. Plan:
1) run matrix across 1 node, exact model artifact (me)
2) collect perf traces (mira + perf-bot)
3) post flamegraphs and kernel selection logs (jonathan)
4) update bench doc with methodology (rachel)
I'll start run now and post results.

perf-bot: RUN COMPLETE: thread 1760884321-run-01
Attached summary:
- streaming / fast-drain / forced_fast: p95=130ms, tokens/sec=980, GPU 80%
- streaming / slow-drain / forced_fast: p95=240ms, tokens/sec=520, GPU 45% (backpressure!)
- blocking / fast-drain / forced_fast: p95=110ms, tokens/sec=1000
- blocking / slow-drain /forced_fast: p95=115ms, tokens/sec=995
Conclusion: streaming is sensitive to client drain; non-streaming hides read latency.

alex_ng: Interesting — confirms the hypothesis. We'll add a note to bench methodology: always run both client read patterns and force kernels when comparing. cc @mira_patel :thumbsup:

infra-ci: logs uploaded to s3://redwood-perf/1760884321/

rachel_wong: I'll turn this into a short how-to section for the eng-runtime bench page and link to logs.

alex_ng: Thanks all, will follow up with PR for bench docs and perf graphs.
